blocks.text: Abstraction. A model exposing relevant operations and guarantees while hiding some implementation details. A queue abstraction defines FIFO behavior; a ring buffer is one possible representation of it. The abstraction should not promise guarantees the representation does not maintain.

blocks.text: Amortized cost. A bound on the total cost of a sequence of operations expressed per operation. It is not a probability claim and does not mean each individual operation has the same latency. Geometric dynamic-array growth is the recurring example in this book.
rich: A bound on the total cost of a sequence of operations expressed per operation. It is not a probability claim and does not mean each individual operation has the same latency. Geometric dynamic-array growth is the recurring example in this book.

blocks.text: Asymptotic bound. A statement about growth as an input measure increases. It requires a chosen cost model and input-size definition. Big-O is an upper bound; it does not automatically specify a tight bound or a particular best, average, or worst case.
rich: A statement about growth as an input measure increases. It requires a chosen cost model and input-size definition. Big-O is an upper bound; it does not automatically specify a tight bound or a particular best, average, or worst case.

blocks.text: Borrow. Access to an object owned elsewhere without taking ownership of its lifetime. References, pointers, iterators, and spans can act as borrows. The borrower must obey both lifetime and invalidation rules; non-nullness alone is not a lifetime proof.
rich: Access to an object owned elsewhere without taking ownership of its lifetime. References, pointers, iterators, and spans can act as borrows. The borrower must obey both lifetime and invalidation rules; non-nullness alone is not a lifetime proof.

blocks.text: Certificate or witness. Additional information allowing a claimed result to be checked. A route’s vertices can demonstrate feasibility and cost. A feasible route alone does not demonstrate that no cheaper route exists.
rich: Additional information allowing a claimed result to be checked. A route’s vertices can demonstrate feasibility and cost. A feasible route alone does not demonstrate that no cheaper route exists.

blocks.text: Commit point. The transition at which a completed candidate replaces accepted state. Preparing a candidate first can preserve the old state on failure. The guarantee must name which state is protected; input consumption and external output are separate effects.
rich: The transition at which a completed candidate replaces accepted state. Preparing a candidate first can preserve the old state on failure. The guarantee must name which state is protected; input consumption and external output are separate effects.

blocks.text: Comparator equivalence. Two values are equivalent under an ordering when neither compares before the other. This can differ from operator==. Ordered containers and sorting stability must be understood in terms of the comparator actually supplied.

blocks.text: Complete search. An exploration that accounts for every solution allowed by its model, either directly or through justified reductions. A heuristic that finds a useful result quickly is not automatically complete.
rich: An exploration that accounts for every solution allowed by its model, either directly or through justified reductions. A heuristic that finds a useful result quickly is not automatically complete.

blocks.text: Differential testing. Comparing multiple implementations or models on the same inputs. Independence matters: two implementations sharing an incorrect recurrence may agree while both solve the wrong problem.
rich: Comparing multiple implementations or models on the same inputs. Independence matters: two implementations sharing an incorrect recurrence may agree while both solve the wrong problem.

blocks.text: Invariant. A property maintained at a designated boundary, such as before every loop iteration or after every public mutation. An invariant is useful when it explains what the representation means and supports the next operation, not merely when it restates that the program should work.
rich: A property maintained at a designated boundary, such as before every loop iteration or after every public mutation. An invariant is useful when it explains what the representation means and supports the next operation, not merely when it restates that the program should work.

blocks.text: Invalidation. The loss of a borrow’s permitted relationship to a container after an operation. Reallocation can invalidate vector iterators even if a high-level operation later reports failure elsewhere. Logical value preservation and borrow preservation are distinct guarantees.
rich: The loss of a borrow’s permitted relationship to a container after an operation. Reallocation can invalidate vector iterators even if a high-level operation later reports failure elsewhere. Logical value preservation and borrow preservation are distinct guarantees.

blocks.text: Optimal substructure. A property allowing an optimal solution to be assembled from appropriate optimal subproblem solutions. The chosen state must contain every constraint affecting future decisions.
rich: A property allowing an optimal solution to be assembled from appropriate optimal subproblem solutions. The chosen state must contain every constraint affecting future decisions.

blocks.text: Partition boundary. A position dividing a sequence according to a predicate. Lower-bound search returns such a boundary; it does not by itself prove that a matching element exists at that position.
rich: A position dividing a sequence according to a predicate. Lower-bound search returns such a boundary; it does not by itself prove that a matching element exists at that position.

blocks.text: Pruning. Omitting a search branch because a justified condition proves that it cannot contribute a required solution. Changing candidate order is a heuristic ordering decision, not necessarily pruning.
rich: Omitting a search branch because a justified condition proves that it cannot contribute a required solution. Changing candidate order is a heuristic ordering decision, not necessarily pruning.

blocks.text: Stability. Preservation of relative order among records equivalent under the sorting comparator. It must be observed with identities or additional fields; sorting equal integers cannot expose an exchange of their indistinguishable positions.
rich: Preservation of relative order among records equivalent under the sorting comparator. It must be observed with identities or additional fields; sorting equal integers cannot expose an exchange of their indistinguishable positions.

blocks.text: State sufficiency. The property that equal state descriptions imply equal future subproblems under the fixed context. A memoization key that omits remaining inventory can violate this property even when its numeric amount matches.
rich: The property that equal state descriptions imply equal future subproblems under the fixed context. A memoization key that omits remaining inventory can violate this property even when its numeric amount matches.

blocks.text: Strict improvement. Replacing a candidate only when its objective value is better, not merely equal. In HarborRoutes this rule supports a simple deterministic predecessor policy and avoids rewriting equal-distance ancestry casually.
rich: Replacing a candidate only when its objective value is better, not merely equal. In HarborRoutes this rule supports a simple deterministic predecessor policy and avoids rewriting equal-distance ancestry casually.

blocks.text: Tombstone. A deleted-slot marker that preserves an open-addressing probe path. It is available for future insertion but does not mean that lookup can stop as it would at a never-used slot.
rich: A deleted-slot marker that preserves an open-addressing probe path. It is available for future insertion but does not mean that lookup can stop as it would at a never-used slot.

topics.title: Review an implementation before relying on it
topics.summary: Write the public contract in ordinary language and make the error model visible. State the accepted sizes, duplicate policy, ordering assumptions, graph direction, arithmetic bounds, and ownership relationships. Include the meaning of empty input and missing results. A precise small contract is more useful than a broad promise the implementation cannot defend.

blocks.headingContext: Review an implementation before relying on it

blocks.text: Trace the representation through one successful operation and one rejected operation. Identify the invariant before and after each mutation. For ownership-changing code, draw which object owns each allocation and which pointers merely observe it. For a loop, name the progress measure and termination condition.
rich: Trace the representation through one successful operation and one rejected operation. Identify the invariant before and after each mutation. For ownership-changing code, draw which object owns each allocation and which pointers merely observe it. For a loop, name the progress measure and termination condition.
blocks.headingContext: Review an implementation before relying on it

blocks.text: Inspect the tests as evidence rather than as a percentage. Look for independent expected results, edge cases, operation histories, failure injection where appropriate, and returned witnesses. Record the compiler and configuration under which they ran. A large count of repeated easy checks does not compensate for one omitted critical transition.
rich: Inspect the tests as evidence rather than as a percentage. Look for independent expected results, edge cases, operation histories, failure injection where appropriate, and returned witnesses. Record the compiler and configuration under which they ran. A large count of repeated easy checks does not compensate for one omitted critical transition.
blocks.headingContext: Review an implementation before relying on it

blocks.text: Finally review performance at the correct boundary. Include preparation and conversion costs when the application pays them. Separate correctness instrumentation from release measurement. A proposed optimization should preserve the required values and failure behavior, improve a relevant measured outcome, and leave a maintainable implementation. When the evidence does not justify a change, retaining the simpler version is a legitimate engineering result.
